tldr: This paper proposes DRILL, a bilevel framework that trains world models not to produce visually pleasing videos, but with a meta-objective: how much reinforcement learning inside them can improve downstream policies. The authors demonstrate that task success rates can increase by up to 13.1 points even when pixel prediction error gets 17% worse.
hero_caption: Overall view of the DRILL framework. In the inner loop, policies are updated via GRPO using imagined rollouts inside the world model, and the resulting learning signals feed back into the outer loop. Two variants are provided: DRILL-VWI, a lightweight reweighting version requiring no additional simulator rollouts, and DRILL-IMG, a high-precision version that backpropagates through the policy update to compute meta-gradients from real simulator returns.
overview:
When post-training robot vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning, "in-mind simulations" (imagined rollouts) using video world models (WMs) have attracted strong attention to cut down on costly interactions with real hardware or simulators. However, conventional world models are fundamentally trained to predict the next frame's pixels accurately (minimizing pixel MSE). This creates a critical Objective Mismatch. Accurately predicting the background or task-irrelevant robot geometry is useless if the model cannot generate learning signals that actually improve the policy. Taken to the extreme, a model with worse pixel prediction that guides policy updates in the right direction is far more useful to a robot.

To address this, the authors propose DRILL (Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop), a bilevel framework that directly optimizes the world model for downstream task performance: how high a return the policy trained inside it achieves in the final target environment. In the inner loop, the policy undergoes GRPO updates on imagined rollouts inside the model; in the outer loop, the world model is updated to maximize the return achieved in the simulator by the updated policy. The authors provide two practical implementations: DRILL-VWI, a lightweight closed-form surrogate requiring zero extra environment collection, and DRILL-IMG, which estimates meta-gradients via short truncated backpropagation through time (BPTT). They also theoretically show that VWI serves as a first-order approximation of IMG.

Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones ($\pi_0$-3B and OpenVLA-7B), DRILL-IMG improved the mean success rate by 13.1 points over existing WMPO and by 7.9 points over RLVR-World. Remarkably, the world model's pixel prediction error (MSE) on the next frame degraded by 17% at the same time. In short, producing visually faithful videos and building smarter policies are two different things, proving that training world models directly with policy gradient signals is an extremely promising direction.
contributions: Formalized the fundamental Objective Mismatch in VLA reinforcement learning between world model pixel prediction accuracy and the utility of the resulting policy gradients.

Proposed DRILL, a bilevel optimization framework that maximizes downstream returns after policy updates on imagined rollouts inside the model, deriving both DRILL-VWI (requiring zero environment rollouts) and DRILL-IMG (computing meta-gradients).
Theoretically proved that DRILL-VWI is a first-order Taylor approximation of DRILL-IMG, and established non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for DRILL-IMG under truncated BPTT.

Defined PUR (Policy-Utility Residual), a method-agnostic diagnostic metric measuring the angular misalignment between pixel MSE gradients and policy improvement directions, showing that low PUR strongly correlates with downstream success rates ($\rho_S = -0.89$).

sections.heading: Predicting clean pixels is not the same as raising smart robots
sections.summary: Video world models are widely used for RL in VLA policies, but a major objective mismatch exists between minimizing pixel MSE and improving policies. Capturing transitions that dictate task success is far more critical than accurately predicting irrelevant background pixels. The authors propose DRILL to train world models using downstream returns from policies learned in imagination.
sections.details:
When fine-tuning robot Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models with reinforcement learning, millions of interaction steps in real environments are prohibitively expensive. Recently, methods that let policies learn by trial and error inside video world models pre-trained on offline demonstration data (such as WMPO) have become mainstream.

However, there is a fundamental catch. World models have traditionally been trained to predict the next frame's pixels—that is, to minimize pixel MSE. Pixel MSE penalizes prediction errors on background textures, robot arm geometry, and task-irrelevant regions completely uniformly. In contrast, what truly matters for policy reinforcement learning (policy gradient methods) are the states the current policy actually visits and the transitions where the advantage (relative action-value) is large. In other words, even if the rendered frames are visually degraded, a world model that guides the direction of policy improvement correctly is what is truly needed.

To resolve this objective mismatch, the paper proposes DRILL (Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop). DRILL employs a bilevel learning loop: the inner loop updates the policy for one step via GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization, an RL method updating policies with group-relative rewards) within the current world model's imagination, while the outer loop optimizes the world model based on how high a return the updated policy achieves in the actual target environment.

DRILL offers two practical variants. One is DRILL-VWI, a lightweight surrogate requiring zero additional simulator sampling. The other is DRILL-IMG, which directly computes meta-gradients using a small amount of simulator rollouts and short truncated BPTT (backpropagation through time). In experiments, models trained with DRILL significantly boosted downstream task success rates, even as their pixel MSE worsened by 17%.

sections.heading: From video generators to policy trainers: how it differs from prior work
sections.summary: Existing world models for VLAs have focused on improving prediction accuracy or rewards for correctness (RLVR), without training models directly on the policy update signal itself. Meanwhile, insights from value-aware model learning and meta-gradients in model-based RL existed, but had never been applied at the 1B+ parameter foundation model scale. DRILL bridges this gap.
sections.details:
Recently, methods like WMPO, VLAW, and WoVR have established pipelines that pretrain video world models from demonstrations and run RL such as GRPO inside them. However, their primary focus remains on improving the model's generative capability (next-frame prediction). Other efforts like RLVR-World use prediction correctness as a reward to train world models with RL, but this still merely refines predictor accuracy without directly evaluating whether the model is useful for policy updates.

On the other hand, the philosophy that "models should be useful for control" has a long history in reinforcement learning, explored in Value-Aware Model Learning, DreamerV3, MuZero, and related works. Yet these rely on bootstrapping value functions $V(s)$, making them difficult to apply directly to massive video generation models. DRILL realizes this philosophy without extra value function learning by directly leveraging the group-relative advantages generated online by GRPO.

Furthermore, scaling meta-gradient techniques (such as MAML and iMAML)—which update outer parameters through an inner optimization process—to combinations of 1B+ parameter video world models and foundation VLA models for the first time represents a major novelty of this work.

sections.heading: Inside DRILL: training policies in imagination, refining models on the results
sections.summary: DRILL performs inner GRPO policy updates on imagined rollouts and maximizes the updated policy's target environment return in the outer loop. It provides two operational modes: DRILL-VWI, requiring no additional simulator calls, and DRILL-IMG, which estimates meta-gradients via truncated Hessian-vector products.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation
Let $\pi_\theta$ denote the VLA policy, $\mathcal{W}_\phi$ the video world model parameterized by $\phi$, and $r_\psi$ a frozen vision-language reward model. In conventional methods (such as WMPO), $\mathcal{W}_\phi$ is trained on demonstration data using pixel reconstruction error (MSE), and policy $\pi_\theta$ is trained with RL inside that model.

### 3.2 DRILL Objective
DRILL fundamentally changes this division of labor. First, let $\pi_{\theta^+(\phi)}$ denote the policy updated after one step of GRPO on imagined rollouts from world model $\mathcal{W}_\phi$. The outer loop objective $J$ of DRILL is the expected return achieved by this updated policy $\pi_{\theta^+(\phi)}$ in the target environment (the simulator). Instead of letting the world model self-evaluate, it optimizes model parameters $\phi$ using true task success in the real environment as feedback.

### 3.3 DRILL-VWI (Visitation-Weighted Imagination)
Because computing meta-gradients at every step is computationally expensive, the authors first derived DRILL-VWI, an alternative loss requiring zero extra environment rollouts. It dynamically reweights (rescales) uniform pixel MSE by the product of three factors:
- Imagined policy visitation $\widehat{\tilde{d}}_\phi^{\pi_\theta}(o_t)$: emphasizes important states frequently visited by the current policy.
- Group-relative advantage $\hat{A}(o_t, a_t)$: a signed quality signal obtained from GRPO. It boosts accuracy on transitions from good actions while downweighting (or pushing away) transitions from bad actions.
- Model confidence $s(o_t)$: suppresses penalties in collapsed states with excessively high uncertainty.
Since all of these quantities are accessible within the imagination loop, this serves as a plug-in surrogate without extra environment interaction.

### 3.4 DRILL-IMG (Implicit Meta-Gradient)
To maximize downstream returns more faithfully, DRILL-IMG backpropagates the gradient of target environment returns through the inner GRPO update rule. By the chain rule, it computes the product of the policy gradient in the target environment and the mixed second-order derivative (Hessian-vector product, or HVP) through the imagined GRPO update. To keep computational costs low, it combines $K$-step (default $K=2$) truncated BPTT with just $B_{\mathrm{real}}=30$ simulator episodes per outer step to estimate meta-gradients efficiently.

captions.F1: Overall architecture of DRILL. (1) Generates imagined rollouts from past observations and instructions. (2) Runs GRPO in the inner loop to extract policy updates and guidance signals. (3) DRILL-VWI reweights prediction errors by advantage, visitation, and confidence. (4) DRILL-IMG backpropagates return gradients from a small number of simulator rollouts into the model via HVP.

sections.heading: Why does this weighting work? Theory connects the two methods
sections.summary: The authors prove that DRILL-VWI is a first-order Taylor approximation of DRILL-IMG, specifying the conditions under which VWI functions effectively. They also guarantee that DRILL-IMG's truncated BPTT bias decays geometrically with step count, ensuring non-asymptotic convergence, and introduce PUR as an objective diagnostic metric.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Theoretical Connection between DRILL-VWI and DRILL-IMG
Proposition 1 addresses why simply reweighting MSE by advantage can substitute for meta-gradients. Assuming local score-compatibility (consistency between changes in model predictions and changes in policy gradients) and small trajectory residuals, the gradient of the DRILL-VWI loss matches the first-order Taylor expansion of the local one-step component of the true meta-gradient sought by DRILL-IMG. In short, DRILL-VWI is not a mere heuristic, but a mathematically derived first-order surrogate for meta-gradients. In regimes with short horizons or high demonstration coverage, VWI provides an adequate approximation without computing expensive meta-gradients.

### 4.2 Convergence Guarantees under Truncated BPTT
DRILL-IMG truncates BPTT at $K$ steps to reduce compute, but does the resulting estimation bias cause problems? Theorem 1 proves that under spectral radius $\rho < 1$ of the inner loop Jacobian, the bias decays geometrically as $B\rho^K$. This guarantees non-asymptotic convergence of stochastic gradient ascent to the neighborhood of a stationary point. This provides theoretical justification that a very shallow truncation of $K=2$ is sufficiently accurate in practice.

### 4.3 Diagnostic Metric: PUR (Policy-Utility Residual)
To objectively measure how orthogonal or counterproductive any world model's training objective is relative to policy improvement, the authors define PUR:
$$\mathrm{PUR} = 1 + \cos\angle(\nabla_\phi \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MSE}}, \nabla_\phi J)$$
If the gradient directions align perfectly, $\mathrm{PUR} \approx 0$; if orthogonal, $\approx 1$; and if completely opposing, $\approx 2$. Because PUR is estimated independently on simulators using finite differences, it serves as a fair, method-agnostic diagnostic benchmark.

sections.heading: Experimental results: pixel accuracy drops 17%, yet success rate jumps 13.1 points
sections.summary: Evaluated across five manipulation benchmarks, DRILL-IMG outperformed WMPO by an average of 13.1 points and RLVR-World by 7.9 points in success rate. Prediction MSE worsened by 17%, clearly illustrating an inversion between pixel accuracy and policy competence. Clear practical guidelines also emerged for choosing between VWI and IMG based on horizon length.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on five simulator environments: LIBERO-Long, CALVIN (ABC$\to$D), RoboCasa, Meta-World MT50, and SimplerEnv. The policy backbones were $\pi_0$-3B and OpenVLA-7B, while the world model used was Ctrl-World (1.2B parameters). Baselines included GRPO from scratch, WMPO, VLAW, RLVR-World, and a model-free baseline matched exactly to DRILL-IMG's simulator run count (Sim-PPO: only 30 trials per outer step).

### 5.2 Main Results: The Pixel MSE Paradox
In average success rate across the five environments with $\pi_0$-3B, DRILL-IMG gained 13.1 points over WMPO and surpassed the strong RLVR-World baseline by 7.9 points. Remarkably, one-step-ahead pixel prediction MSE on the exact same training data was 17% higher (worse) for DRILL-IMG than for the baseline. By abandoning uniform pixel matching and selectively warping the transitions that are critical for policy improvement, the robot's actual task performance grew dramatically.

Applying DRILL-IMG to a world model pretrained with RLVR-World further boosted success rate by 3.2 points, demonstrating that prediction correctness and policy-oriented meta-optimization are complementary rather than mutually exclusive.

### 5.3 Ablation and Scaling
Ablating the three components of DRILL-VWI individually showed that "visitation only" achieved 64.2%, "advantage only" reached 66.8%, and "confidence only" yielded 60.1%, whereas the fully integrated DRILL-VWI reached 69.2% (compared to WMPO at 58.2%). Furthermore, scaling the world model from 300M to 1.2B and 7B parameters widened DRILL-IMG's lead over WMPO from 7.9pt $\to$ 13.1pt $\to$ 16.4pt, confirming that larger model capacity yields even greater benefits.

### 5.4 Choosing Between DRILL-VWI and DRILL-IMG
Given computational overhead (IMG consumes roughly 1.4$\times$ the compute time of VWI plus 30 simulator rollouts per step), which should one use? Experiments varying horizon length $H$ provide a clear answer. In SimplerEnv where episodes are short (effective $H < 20$), performance between DRILL-VWI (64.0%) and DRILL-IMG (63.1%) is virtually identical. Conversely, on long tasks like LIBERO-Long ($H=50\sim 100$), IMG demonstrates a decisive advantage: at $H=100$, DRILL-IMG reaches 83.4%, leaving VWI far behind. Therefore, DRILL-VWI is ideal for short horizons or zero environment access, while DRILL-IMG is the top choice for long-horizon tasks when modest simulator access is allowed.

### 5.5 Diagnostics and Robustness
Tracking PUR (Policy-Utility Residual) over time revealed that while WMPO's PUR worsened as training progressed (diverging from the policy improvement direction), DRILL-IMG steadily decreased PUR, showing an extremely strong negative correlation of $\rho_S = -0.89$ with downstream success rate. In a blind human study (120 trials), participants found visual video quality indistinguishable between methods, but 62% preferred DRILL-IMG rollouts for clearly visualizing task completion.

sections.heading: Conclusion: training world models for educational utility, not visual appearance
sections.summary: DRILL shifts the optimization target of video world models from traditional frame prediction accuracy to the downstream return of the trained policy. Despite limitations such as simulation-only evaluation and meta-gradient compute costs, this represents a crucial step against the convention of pursuing visual fidelity alone.
sections.details:
This work proposed DRILL, a bilevel optimization framework for training video world models not merely as high-fidelity video generators, but as the best simulation environments for nurturing policies. Offering two variants—the lightweight weighted surrogate DRILL-VWI and implicit meta-gradient DRILL-IMG—it demonstrated that policy success rates can improve significantly even when pixel prediction MSE deteriorates.

### Limitations and Future Work
The paper candidly outlines the following limitations:
- All evaluations were conducted in simulation, leaving real-robot deployment unexamined. Robustness to real-world sensory noise, actuation delays, and the Sim-to-Real gap remains to be tested.
- DRILL-IMG requires a small number of simulator rollouts, and calculating HVPs introduces additional memory overhead and compute cost.
Extending the framework to real-robot post-training and developing even lighter meta-gradient estimators represent important future steps.

sections.heading: Appendix: algorithm stabilization tricks and computational costs behind the scenes
sections.summary: Details implementation techniques to compute HVPs stably on 1B-scale models (memory reduction via VJPs, float32 accumulation, gradient clipping), compute resource breakdowns (17k H20-hours), and the random-projection algorithm used to estimate PUR.
sections.details:
- Memory-Efficient HVP Implementation: To avoid explicitly expanding the massive $|\phi| \times |\theta|$ mixed Hessian matrix, it is implemented via vector-Jacobian products (VJPs). Computation graphs are retained (create_graph=True) only for the first $K$ steps of imagined rollouts, while the remaining $H-K$ steps run under torch.no_grad(), cutting peak memory by roughly 25$\times$ compared to full BPTT.
- Ensuring Numerical Stability: When running meta-gradients on 1B+ video models, outer gradient norms are clipped to 10, and HVP inner-product accumulations are strictly performed in float32 rather than bfloat16 (as bfloat16 diverged mid-training). Normalization statistics of the world model are frozen during outer updates.
- Random-Projection PUR Estimation: To evaluate outer return gradients $\nabla_\phi J$ without reusing DRILL-IMG machinery, a two-point finite difference method along $r=128$ random Gaussian directions is employed. Using common random numbers (same seeds and initial states) reduces estimation variance by 1–2 orders of magnitude.
- Compute Cost Breakdown: Across all main experiments, approximately 17,000 NVIDIA H20-hours were consumed (about 4 weeks across 24 GPUs). The additional cost of DRILL-IMG over an existing WMPO pipeline comes solely from outer-loop computation, accounting for roughly 3,800 H20-hours.

takeaways: A low pixel prediction MSE in a world model does not guarantee an effective policy training environment; worse MSE and higher task performance can go hand in hand.
Reweighting prediction errors by current policy visitation and advantage is remarkably effective for shaping world models that actually produce smarter policies.
Practitioners should choose the lightweight DRILL-VWI for short horizons or zero-environment-access regimes, and switch to DRILL-IMG for long horizons when modest simulator access is acceptable.
Methods rewarding model prediction correctness (such as RLVR) and DRILL's policy-improving meta-gradients are not mutually exclusive; combining them yields even greater complementary gains.
limitations: All experiments are restricted to simulator environments (LIBERO, CALVIN, etc.), leaving resilience to real-robot noise and the Sim-to-Real gap unvalidated.
DRILL-IMG requires a small batch of simulator rollouts in the outer loop (30 trajectories per step), departing from purely offline training regimes.
Truncated BPTT and Hessian-vector product (HVP) calculations introduce additional GPU memory consumption and computational time overhead.
